\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:responding}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how someone is in Kannada, answer naturally, and return the question.}

Run the whole exchange: nīvu hēgiddīrā? — nānu cennāgiddēne, dhanyavāda — and wave away the thanks with paravāgilla.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hēge]{\kn{ಹೇಗೆ} (hēge) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} another of the ē- questions}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-hege}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{\kn{ಏನು}} (\emph{ēnu}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) in Chapter 2. Here is its sibling in Kannada's question family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)} \textbf{\kn{ಹೇ}} (\emph{hē}, \emph{ha} + the long-\emph{ē} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ಗೆ}} (\emph{ge}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಹೇಗೆ}} (\emph{hēge}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೇಗೆ}} (\emph{hēge}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative base \textbf{ē-/yā-} you met in \emph{ēnu}. Kannada gathers its questions here: \emph{ēnu} (what), \emph{hēge} (how), \emph{yāru} (who), \emph{elli} (where), \emph{yāvāga} (when), \emph{yāke} (why). It is the same Dravidian question-root heading Tamil's \emph{eppaṭi} and Telugu's \emph{elā} — a family far older than the Sanskrit words Kannada, like its sisters, borrows so readily.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}hēge\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the question family — \emph{ēnu, hēge, yāru, elli, yāvāga}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sari}, then read \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}}, then say \emph{nanna}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What base do Kannada's question-words share, and which cousins head their own? (The interrogative \emph{ē-/yā-}; Tamil's \emph{eppaṭi}, Telugu's \emph{elā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[virama]{\kn{◌್} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S03-sign-virama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ು} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌್}}
\textbf{\kn{◌್}} — \emph{no sound of its own — it takes one away}.

It is a \textbf{vowel-killer}. Every consonant in this script arrives with an \emph{a} already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the \emph{a} back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌್} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} — hello / greetings (namaskāra — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}} \emph{dhanyavāda} — thank you (dhanyavāda — \textquotedblleft{}an utterance of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} \emph{illa} — no / there isn't (illa — the negative)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ}} \emph{nanna} — my
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌್} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌್} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌್} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}  ·  \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}  ·  \kn{ಹೌದು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌್} three times, and each time say what it does: \textbf{it kills the built-in \emph{a}}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌್} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{◌್}? What does it do to the consonant it sits on? (\textbf{Takes away the built-in \emph{a}.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nīvu hēgiddīrā]{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}? (nīvu hēgiddīrā?)}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-niivu-hegiddiira}



\begin{quote}
The everyday \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and the verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} that carries it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
The new word is \textbf{\kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}} (\emph{hēgiddīrā}): \emph{hēge} (\textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) fused with \textbf{\kn{ಇದ್ದೀರಾ}} (\emph{iddīrā}, \textquotedblleft{}are you\textquotedblright{}), from the verb \textbf{\kn{ಇರು}} (\emph{iru}, \textquotedblleft{}to be, exist, stay\textquotedblright{}) + the respectful-you ending. Note the doubled \textbf{\kn{ದ್ದ}} (\emph{dd}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} = \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು}} (\emph{nīvu}, \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful) + \textbf{\kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}} (\emph{hēgiddīrā}, \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{}) — the verb \textbf{last}, as always. The verb is \textbf{\kn{ಇರು}} (\emph{iru}, \textquotedblleft{}to be / exist / stay\textquotedblright{}) — the same native Dravidian \emph{iru} that Tamil uses for \textquotedblleft{}how are you,\textquotedblright{} and (in Chapter 5) the verb for \textquotedblleft{}I live.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb carries \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}]
The ending already means \textquotedblleft{}you (respectful),\textquotedblright{} so \emph{nīvu} can be dropped: \emph{hēgiddīrā?} alone is a complete \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} To a friend (\emph{nīnu}), it shifts: \textbf{\kn{ನೀನು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀಯಾ}?} (\emph{nīnu hēgiddīyā?}). Match the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to the verb-ending, as Kannada always does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful question — \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?}
  \item the familiar version — \emph{nīnu hēgiddīyā?}
  \item the verb and its meaning (\emph{iru} — \textquotedblleft{}to be / exist / stay\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb powers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}, and which Dravidian sister uses the same one? (\emph{Iru}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}; Tamil — its \emph{iru} is the same word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nānu]{\kn{ನಾನು} (nānu) — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the Dravidian first person}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-naanu}



\begin{quote}
To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} you first need \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} In Chapter 2 you learned \emph{nanna} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}); here is its owner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾ}} (\emph{nā}, \emph{na} + long-\emph{ā} sign) + \textbf{\kn{ನು}} (\emph{nu}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ನಾನು}} (\emph{nānu}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾನು}} (\emph{nānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*yāṉ / *nāṉ} — native, and (unlike Hindi's \emph{maiṁ}, cousin of English \emph{me}) \textbf{not} related to the European \textquotedblleft{}I/me\textquotedblright{} family. Its possessive is the \textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ}} (\emph{nanna}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) you already met: \emph{nānu} \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} \emph{nanna} \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} Kannada borrows Sanskrit words freely for higher vocabulary, but its bedrock pronouns stayed Dravidian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} you can drop}]
Kannada verbs carry the person in their ending — \emph{iddēne} already means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} am\textquotedblright{} — so \emph{nānu} is often left out. You still learn it first, because the answer to \emph{hēgiddīrā?} begins with it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair — \emph{nānu} (I), \emph{nanna} (my)
  \item \emph{Say it:} is it related to English \emph{me}? (No — native Dravidian)
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ನೀನು} / \kn{ನೀವು}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{nānu}'s possessive, and is Kannada's \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} cousin to English \emph{me}? (\emph{Nanna}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}; no — it is native Dravidian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cennāgi]{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ} (cennāgi) — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-cennaagi}



\begin{quote}
The word that answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and it means, at heart, \textquotedblleft{}beautifully.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ಚೆ}} (\emph{ce} — the letter \textbf{\kn{ಚ}} is \textquotedblleft{}ch as in \emph{cheese},\textquotedblright{} so this sounds like \textquotedblleft{}che\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ನ್ನಾ}} (\emph{nnā}, doubled \emph{n} + long \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\kn{ಗಿ}} (\emph{gi}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ}} (\emph{cennāgi}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ}} (\emph{cennāgi}, \textquotedblleft{}well, nicely\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, from \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನು}} (\emph{cennu}, \textquotedblleft{}good, beautiful, fine\textquotedblright{}) + the adverb-maker \emph{-āgi} (\textquotedblleft{}in a … way\textquotedblright{}). So it literally means \textquotedblleft{}in a beautiful way\textquotedblright{} — Kannada answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} by saying, in effect, \textquotedblleft{}beautifully.\textquotedblright{} The root \emph{cennu} is pure Kannada, with no Sanskrit or European cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The reply}
Fuse it with the \emph{iru} verb: \textbf{\kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ}} (\emph{nānu cennāgiddēne}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am well}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{cennāgi} + \emph{iddēne}, \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}). The whole exchange:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?} (\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{nānu cennāgiddēne, dhanyavāda.} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}cennāgi\textquotedblright{} (the \kn{ಚ} = \textquotedblleft{}ch\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Say it:} the full reply — \emph{nānu cennāgiddēne}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what \emph{cennu} means at root (\textquotedblleft{}good / beautiful\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēnu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the full reply to \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?}, and say what \emph{cennāgi} literally means. (\emph{Nānu cennāgiddēne}; \textquotedblleft{}in a beautiful way,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{cennu} \textquotedblleft{}good/beautiful.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ga]{\kn{ಗ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S112-letter-ga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ೆ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಗ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗ}} — \emph{ga}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{g}, it is \textbf{ga}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಗ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೇಗೆ}} \emph{hēge} — how
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā} — how are you? (respectful)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ}} \emph{cennāgi} — well, nicely — and the reply \textquotedblleft{}\kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಗ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಗ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಗ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಹೇಗೆ}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಗ} three times, saying \emph{ga} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಗ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಗ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ga}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paravāgilla]{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ} (paravāgilla) — \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-paravaagilla}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, built on a word you met in Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾ}} (\emph{paravā}, \textquotedblleft{}harm, concern\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಗಿಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{gilla}, a fused form of \emph{āgi} + \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} \emph{illa}, \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{paravāgilla}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it does not matter / there is no harm}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{paravā} (\textquotedblleft{}harm, concern\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{illa}, \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{}). It serves as \textquotedblleft{}it's okay / no worries / never mind / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} The key atom, \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{illa}), you met in Chapter 1 — Kannada's word for negation and non-existence, the mirror of \emph{iru} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}). Where \emph{iru} says \textquotedblleft{}it is,\textquotedblright{} \emph{illa} says \textquotedblleft{}it is not.\textquotedblright{} This \emph{illa} is shared, almost unchanged, across \textbf{Kannada, Tamil, and Malayalam} — one of the deep bonds of the Dravidian south. (Telugu alone breaks away, to \emph{lēdu} — so Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{} is \emph{paravālēdu}, Kannada's is \emph{paravāgilla}, each on its own \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{})
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}, the all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}]
\emph{Illa} negates existence and equations alike, and stands alone as \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}: \emph{duḍḍu illa} (\textquotedblleft{}there's no money\textquotedblright{}), \emph{nānu illa} (\textquotedblleft{}it's not me\textquotedblright{}). Hold \emph{iru} / \emph{illa} together — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}is-not.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}paravāgilla\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}it does not matter / no harm\textquotedblright{})
  \item the three Dravidian sisters that share \emph{illa} (Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{paravāgilla} literally say, and which languages share its \emph{illa}? (\textquotedblleft{}There is no harm\textquotedblright{}; Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam — Telugu uses \emph{lēdu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 3 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:KA-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (respectful) — \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nānu cennāgiddēne, dhanyavāda.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}No problem / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{paravāgilla.}
  \item the familiar version of the question — \emph{nīnu hēgiddīyā?}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ē- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{hēge})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} and the verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nānu}, \emph{iru})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}is / is-not\textquotedblright{} pair (\emph{iru} / \emph{illa})
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hēge} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{ē-/yā-} (native Dravidian, like Tamil \emph{eppaṭi})
  \item \emph{nānu} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian (unrelated to English \emph{me}); possessive \emph{nanna}
  \item \emph{cennāgi} $\leftarrow$ \emph{cennu} \textquotedblleft{}good/beautiful\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}in a beautiful way\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{iru} / \emph{illa} — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{}; \emph{illa} shared with Tamil \& Malayalam
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A stranger asks \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?} — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (\emph{Nānu cennāgiddēne, dhanyavāda} — and to thanks, \emph{paravāgilla}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
